name: Merv
subtitle: Marw al-Shahijan, Queen of the World
description: Two thousand years of Merv in the Murghab oasis, where each age built a new walled city beside the last: the round Achaemenid citadel of Erk Kala, the square Hellenistic and Sasanian city of Gyaur Kala, the vast Seljuk city of Sultan Kala round Sanjar's mausoleum, its emptying after the Mongols, and the small Timurid town to the south. Positions are projected from real coordinates; the drawing is an illustration, not a survey.

water.name: Nahr Majan (Majan canal)
water.blurb: The canal of the new city: Abu Muslim built his palace and mosque on its banks in 748, and it ran through the markets of Sultan Kala past the Friday mosque. Its line here is approximate.

water.name: Majan canal (silted)
water.blurb: After 1221 the dams were broken and the canals left uncleaned; the Majan carries a trickle in spring floods.

water.name: Nahr Razik (Razik canal)
water.blurb: One of the four great canals taken off the Murghab, running north along the west side of the old city. Geographers name four: the Hurmuzfarra, Majan, Razik and Asadi; their courses here are schematic.

water.name: Nahr Hurmuzfarra
water.blurb: The westernmost of Merv's four canals, watering the estates and koshks west of the city. Its Persian name recalls a Sasanian founder.

water.name: Nahr Asadi
water.blurb: The eastern canal, watering the fields beyond the old city. Its name may come from Asad ibn Abdallah, Umayyad governor of Khurasan.

water.name: Old canal of Margu
water.blurb: An irrigation channel bringing Murghab water north to the fields below the citadel; the Achaemenid canal system is known only in outline.

hills.name: Mound of Erk Kala
hills.blurb: The citadel stands on a rampart and mound of mud brick that grew with every rebuilding; today it rises some 30 metres above the plain.

hills.name: Edge of the Karakum
hills.blurb: Where the canals failed after 1221 the dunes of the Black Sand desert crept in over the northern fields.

roads.name: Road to the citadel
roads.blurb: The track up from the southern fields and the road to Aria (Herat) to the gate of Erk Kala.

roads.name: Road to Hyrcania
roads.blurb: West across the oasis toward Parthia and Hyrcania by the Caspian.

roads.name: North–south street of Gyaur Kala
roads.blurb: From the south gate to the foot of the citadel. The Hellenistic city was laid out round two main streets crossing at right angles, a plan still visible from the air.

roads.name: East–west street of Gyaur Kala
roads.blurb: Across the city from the west gate to the east gate and the road to the Oxus.

roads.name: Road to Herat
roads.blurb: South up the Murghab valley to Herat and on to Sistan and India.

roads.name: Road to Amul and Bukhara
roads.blurb: North-east across the Karakum to Amul on the Oxus, then Bukhara and Samarkand: the Silk Road eastward.

roads.name: Road to Nishapur
roads.blurb: West to Sarakhs, Nishapur and Ctesiphon: the Great Khurasan Road.

roads.name: Street of the Majan
roads.blurb: The main street of Sultan Kala from the south gate past the Friday mosque and Sanjar's mausoleum to the north gate, running beside the Majan canal.

roads.name: Street of the Shahristan gate
roads.blurb: Across Sultan Kala from the west gate to the east gate facing the old city (the shahristan); street names after the geographers, positions schematic.

roads.name: Road to the old city
roads.blurb: Over the Razik canal to the west gate of Gyaur Kala, by now a half-deserted quarter of potters and brick kilns.

roads.name: Lane through the old city
roads.blurb: The old main street of Gyaur Kala, still the road east to Amul and Bukhara.

roads.name: Road to Nishapur
roads.blurb: West to Sarakhs and Nishapur on the Khurasan Road; caravans from Iraq and Iran came in here.

roads.name: Road to Herat
roads.blurb: South from the main gate up the Murghab valley to Herat.

roads.name: Road to Khwarazm
roads.blurb: North out of the city toward Khwarazm across the desert.

roads.name: Bazaar street of the new town
roads.blurb: The main street of Shah Rukh's town, from the south gate to the north gate.

roads.name: Cross street
roads.blurb: The east–west street crossing at the bazaar.

roads.name: Road to the old cities
roads.blurb: North through the ruins of Sultan Kala, past fields laid out inside its walls.

roads.name: Road to Herat
roads.blurb: South to Herat, Shah Rukh's capital.

roads.name: Road to Mashhad
roads.blurb: West to Sarakhs and Mashhad, where Shah Rukh's wife Gawhar Shad had built her great mosque.

roads.name: Track through the ruins
roads.blurb: A path among the mounds where the main street of Sultan Kala had been, used by herders and pilgrims to Sanjar's tomb.

walls.name: Walls of Erk Kala
walls.blurb: A ring of mud-brick walls on a rampart about 20 hectares round, raised in the Achaemenid period and rebuilt many times; the citadel of every city of Merv until the Seljuks.

walls.name: Rampart of Erk Kala
walls.blurb: The old citadel's rampart, abandoned as the city moved west: a ring of eroded earth inside the old city's north wall.

walls.name: Walls of Gyaur Kala
walls.blurb: The square walls of Antiochia Margiana, thickened by the Parthians and Sasanians into a massive mud-brick rampart with towers, a gallery for archers and four gates in the middle of the sides.

walls.name: Walls of the shahristan (Gyaur Kala)
walls.blurb: Still standing round the old city, now an inner suburb of potters and craftsmen; the Seljuks kept them in repair as a second line of defence.

walls.name: Ruined walls of Gyaur Kala
walls.blurb: Slumped ramparts, their towers rounded into mounds by wind and rain.

walls.name: Walls of Sultan Kala
walls.blurb: Built by Malik Shah about 1080 and strengthened by Sanjar: a high wall of mud brick and pakhsa with half-round towers every 15–30 metres, a lower outer wall and a ditch. Their trace here is simplified.

walls.name: Ruined walls of Sultan Kala
walls.blurb: Breached by the Mongols in 1221 and never repaired; the ramparts still stand many metres high today.

walls.name: Walls of Abdullah Khan Kala
walls.blurb: The walls of the Timurid town, a rough square of about 600 metres with corner towers and gates on the axes; the later name comes from a 16th-century Uzbek ruler.

bridges.name: Bridge over the Razik
bridges.blurb: Where the road west left the old city by its west gate and crossed the Razik canal.

bridges.name: Bridge over the Razik
bridges.blurb: The crossing between the new city and the old, of fired brick.

bridges.name: Bridge of the Majan
bridges.blurb: The main cross street bridging the Majan canal in the heart of Sultan Kala.

bridges.name: Bridge over the Asadi
bridges.blurb: A timber bridge on the road to Amul and the desert crossing.

gardens.name: Orchards south of the old city

districts.name: Erk Kala
districts.description: The round citadel of Margu: governor's residence, granaries and soldiers' houses behind a high rampart.

districts.name: Gyaur Kala (Antiochia Margiana)
districts.description: The square city of the Seleucids, Parthians and Sasanians, with Erk Kala as its citadel: houses, workshops, temples, a stupa and churches along a grid of streets.

districts.name: The shahristan (Gyaur Kala)
districts.description: The old walled city, emptying as people moved west to the Majan; kilns, workshops and a few mosques remain.

districts.name: Sultan Kala
districts.description: The Seljuk city west of the old one: the Shahriyar Ark, the Friday mosque and Sanjar's mausoleum, markets, libraries and dense courtyard houses along the Majan canal.

districts.name: Ruins of Sultan Kala
districts.description: The great Seljuk city after 1221: empty courtyards, slumped walls and the lone dome of Sanjar's mausoleum.

districts.name: Abdullah Khan Kala
districts.description: Shah Rukh's new town south of the old cities, walled and laid out on two cross streets.

periods.label: Margu, satrapy of Margiana
periods.summary: Margu, the Margiana of the Greeks, is a province of the Persian Empire, named in Darius' inscription at Behistun. Its stronghold is Erk Kala, a round citadel of mud brick on a high rampart above the irrigated delta of the Murghab, where the oasis river fans out into canals before dying in the Karakum sands. Around it lie farmsteads, fields and vineyards.
periods.population: unknown; a few thousand in and around the citadel
periods.feel: Donkeys on the rampart ramp, the creak of water-lifts on the canals, Persian officials counting barley tax in the citadel yard, desert wind carrying sand over the fields.

houses.title: Houses inside Erk Kala
houses.text: Small mud-brick houses round yards, packed inside the citadel rampart and roofed with poplar beams, reed mats and clay; storerooms for grain and a hearth in every house.

outskirts.title: Farmsteads of the delta
outskirts.text: Scattered farmsteads with thick mud walls, each by its own canal: wheat, barley, millet and vines, flocks driven to the desert edge in spring.

periods.label: Marw of the Sasanians
periods.summary: Refounded about 280 BCE by Antiochus I as Antiochia Margiana, the city is now Gyaur Kala, a walled square nearly two kilometres a side with Erk Kala as its citadel. Under the Sasanians it is a frontier capital and mint. Fire temples, a Buddhist stupa and monastery and the churches of a Christian metropolitan stand inside one wall: a city of many faiths. Mud brick and pakhsa.
periods.population: unknown; perhaps a few tens of thousands
periods.feel: Hymns in Syriac from the church, chanting at the Buddhist monastery, the smoke of the sacred fire, Sogdian, Persian and Bactrian spoken at the caravan gates.

houses.title: Houses of Gyaur Kala
houses.text: Mud-brick and pakhsa courtyard houses along a grid of lanes between the two main streets, flat roofs of beams and clay, workshops of potters, glass- and metalworkers in their own quarters.

outskirts.title: Koshks and villages
outskirts.text: Outside the walls the estates of the landed gentry (dihqans), each a fortified koshk with corrugated walls, among canals, orchards and the villages of the oasis.

periods.label: Seljuk metropolis
periods.summary: Taken by the Seljuk Turks in 1037, Merv (Marw al-Shahijan) is the capital of Khurasan and from 1118 of Sultan Sanjar's empire. The city has moved west of the old walls to Sultan Kala, walled by the Seljuks, with the Shahriyar Ark, the Friday mosque, libraries Yaqut would praise and markets of silk and cotton. Perhaps the largest city in the world about 1150, though estimates differ.
periods.feel: The call to prayer from a dozen minarets, bales of cotton cloth under the bazaar domes, Turkic horsemen at the Ark gate, scholars arguing in the library reading rooms.

houses.title: Courtyard houses of Sultan Kala
houses.text: Mud-brick courtyard houses with flat earth roofs and a domed room or two of fired brick for the well-off; a pool or a channel from the canal in the yard; lanes of workshops grouped by trade near the markets.

outskirts.title: Koshks, ice houses and melon fields
outskirts.text: The oasis round the walls: walled gardens and the corrugated koshks of the gentry, conical ice houses (yakhdan) by the canals, orchards and the famous melon fields.

periods.label: After the Mongols
periods.summary: In February 1221 the Mongol army of Tolui, son of Chinggis Khan, took Merv, drove the people onto the plain and killed most of them; the dams of the Murghab were later broken. Sultan Kala stands empty, its walls slumping, the Ark gutted. Only the mausoleum of Sanjar still raises its dome over the ruins. A small population lingers under the Ilkhans.
periods.feel: Wind through empty gates, jackals in the bazaar, a few families farming among the mounds, travellers stopping to pray at Sanjar's tomb.

houses.title: Squatters in the ruins
houses.text: A few houses patched together from fallen brick in the corners of old courtyards, roofed with reeds; most of the city a field of melted mud walls.

outskirts.title: Fields gone to desert
outskirts.text: With the canals neglected the oasis shrinks: tamarisk and sand over old fields, a few villages where water still runs.

periods.label: Shah Rukh's Merv
periods.summary: Timur's son Shah Rukh orders Merv rebuilt, by the usual account in 1409: the Murghab dam is restored, the canals cleaned, and a new, smaller walled town laid out south of the old cities, later called Abdullah Khan Kala. The old cities to the north are fields, brick quarries and shrines, among them the Askhab mausolea given new Timurid iwans.
periods.feel: Masons cutting new brick from old walls, water running again in the Majan, Turkmen herders selling sheep at the gate, pilgrims at the Companions' tombs.

houses.title: Houses of the new town
houses.text: Mud-brick courtyard houses inside the Timurid walls, an ayvan porch on wooden posts facing the yard, flat roofs where families slept in summer; small mosques and a bazaar on the cross streets.

outskirts.title: Fields among the ruins
outskirts.text: Irrigated fields and melon beds laid out between the walls of the old cities; shepherds' pens in the empty gates of Sultan Kala.

landmarks.name: Mausoleum of Sultan Sanjar

sasanian-500.note: Canal-side fields and gardens west of the walled city. The Seljuk city of Sultan Kala does not yet exist.

seljuk-1100.note: Raised about 1157, late in this era, at the heart of Sultan Kala beside the Friday mosque: Sanjar's tomb, its outer dome said to have been visible a day's ride away.

ruins-1250.note: Looted by the Mongols in 1221 but left standing: the one great building still upright in the emptied city, a landmark for every traveller on the plain.

timurid-1450.note: A shrine among fields and ruins north of Shah Rukh's new town; its outer dome and tiles weathering, the inner dome intact.

landmarks.summary: The tomb of the last great Seljuk sultan, about 1157: a cube of fired brick 27 metres square under an arcaded gallery and a double dome rising some 38 metres.
details: Sanjar (r. 1118–1157) built his tomb in the centre of his capital. A square hall of fired brick carries an octagonal zone and an open gallery of arches, and above it two domes, an inner one painted with stucco and an outer shell. An inscription in the dome names the builder, Muhammad ibn Atsiz of Sarakhs.

The miniature shows the plain lower cube with its blind niches, the gallery of arches round the upper storey, the drum and the outer dome glazed turquoise, as Yaqut and later writers describe it; the tiling is hedged, since only fragments survive. The attached mosque and palace buildings are left out.

landmarks.name: Friday Mosque of Sultan Kala

sasanian-500.note: Fields along the Majan canal. Abu Muslim's first mosque of the new city (748) stood somewhere nearby on the canal.

seljuk-1100.note: The congregational mosque of the Seljuk capital, beside Sanjar's mausoleum, with a library in its care.

ruins-1250.note: Burned and abandoned after 1221: low mounds of brick west of the standing mausoleum.

landmarks.summary: The congregational mosque of Seljuk Merv, next to Sanjar's mausoleum: a court with four iwans and a brick dome over the prayer hall, as the usual Seljuk plan suggests.
details: Writers place Merv's Friday mosque on the Majan canal in the new city, and excavation found a large mosque beside Sanjar's mausoleum. Its full plan is not known. Yaqut says one of Merv's waqf libraries, with some 12,000 volumes, was kept in the Friday mosque.

The miniature follows the four-iwan court mosque of Seljuk Iran (Isfahan, Zavareh): a brick dome chamber on the qibla (west) side, iwans on the axes, arcades round the court and one minaret. It is an interpretation, not a plan of the excavated building.

landmarks.name: Shahriyar Ark

sasanian-500.note: Gardens and fields on the canals west of Gyaur Kala; no citadel here yet.

seljuk-1100.note: The Seljuk citadel in the north-east of Sultan Kala: the sultan's palace, the treasury and a garrison behind its own walls.

ruins-1250.name: Shahriyar Ark (ruined)
ruins-1250.note: Stormed and burned in 1221; the palace roofs gone, the walls breached. Squatters camp in its courts.

timurid-1450.name: Shahriyar Ark (ruined)
timurid-1450.note: An empty walled mound north of the new town, mined for brick.

landmarks.summary: The walled citadel of Seljuk Merv, about 12 hectares in the north-east corner of Sultan Kala, with the palace of the sultans, a pavilion-keep and the curious Kepter Khana.
details: Built in the 11th century and enlarged under Sanjar, the Ark had its own walls with closely set towers. Excavated buildings include a palace of four iwans round a court and the Kepter Khana, a building lined with rows of small niches, explained as a dovecote, a library or a strong-room.

The miniature shows the walls, a gate, the palace court and a tall keep with corrugated walls in the manner of the koshks: that keep, the inner buildings and their arrangement are a reconstruction. The ruined variant follows the mounds seen today.
landmarks.function: Citadel and palace of the Seljuk sultans

landmarks.name: Walls of Sultan Kala (south gate)

sasanian-500.note: Open country on the Herat road; the canals and fields of the western oasis.

seljuk-1100.note: Begun under Malik Shah about 1080 and strengthened by Sanjar: a high wall with towers every few dozen metres, an outer wall, a ditch and a fortified south gate on the Herat road.

ruins-1250.name: Walls of Sultan Kala (breached)
ruins-1250.note: Breached in 1221 and left to the weather: towers slumped into cones, the gate a gap between mounds.

timurid-1450.name: Walls of Sultan Kala (ruined)
timurid-1450.note: Still a tall earthen ridge round fields and ruins; the road from the new town runs through the old gate gap.

landmarks.summary: The massive mud-brick walls of the Seljuk city, with half-round towers set close together, an outer wall and a ditch: here the south gate where the Herat road came in.
details: The Seljuk walls of Sultan Kala ran for several kilometres. Excavation shows a main wall of mud brick and pakhsa on a sloping base, with an inner gallery and arrow-slits, towers at short intervals, a lower outer wall in front and a ditch. The walls were rebuilt several times in the 12th century.

The miniature shows a 300-metre stretch: ditch, outer wall, glacis and main wall with towers about 15 metres apart, and a gate between two big towers. Heights and the gate plan are reconstructed; the ruined variant shows the ridges that still stand.

landmarks.name: Walls of Gyaur Kala (south gate)

achaemenid-500.note: Fields and the road south from Erk Kala. The square city will be laid out here in Hellenistic times.

sasanian-500.name: Walls of Antiochia Margiana
sasanian-500.note: The square city's walls, raised in Hellenistic times and thickened by Parthians and Sasanians, with closely set towers and a gallery for archers.

seljuk-1100.name: Walls of the shahristan
seljuk-1100.note: Still standing round the half-emptied old city, now east of the busy new one.

ruins-1250.name: Ruined walls of Gyaur Kala
ruins-1250.note: Long abandoned walls slumped into ridges, their towers worn round.

timurid-1450.name: Ruined walls of Gyaur Kala
timurid-1450.note: Earthen ridges among fields north of Shah Rukh's town.

landmarks.summary: The walls of Gyaur Kala, the square Hellenistic city of Antiochia Margiana, nearly two kilometres a side, rebuilt over a thousand years; here the south gate.
details: Antiochus I's square city (about 280 BCE) took in Erk Kala as its citadel. Its walls were thickened again and again until they formed a rampart many metres thick, with towers at close intervals and, in Sasanian times, a vaulted gallery for archers inside. A gate in the middle of each side led to the two main streets.
The miniature shows a 240-metre stretch of mud-brick wall on a sloping base, with towers, arrow-slits and a gate flanked by two towers. Details of the gate are reconstructed.
landmarks.built: c. 280 BCE, rebuilt to the 6th century CE

landmarks.name: Beni Makhan Mosque

sasanian-500.note: Houses at the crossing of the two main streets of Gyaur Kala; Islam has not yet reached Merv.

seljuk-1100.note: An old mosque in the half-empty shahristan, still used by the potters and craftsmen who stayed in the old city.

ruins-1250.note: Abandoned; its cistern and walls survive as low mounds near the centre of Gyaur Kala.

landmarks.summary: An early mosque at the centre of Gyaur Kala, traditionally linked with the Arab settlers of the 8th century, with a large cistern beside it.
details: Excavation in the centre of the old city uncovered a mosque and a big domed cistern. Its name is linked with an Arab tribal group (the Banu Mahan); its date is uncertain, usually put in the 8th century and later rebuilt.
The miniature shows a modest court mosque: a flat-roofed prayer hall of piers on the qibla side, an arcaded court, a square minaret and a domed cistern. The plan is a reconstruction.

landmarks.name: Buddhist stupa and monastery

achaemenid-500.note: Fields south of the citadel; Buddhism reaches Merv only centuries later.

sasanian-500.note: A stupa of mud brick on a square base with a monastery of cells beside it, the westernmost Buddhist foundation known in Central Asia.

seljuk-1100.note: Long gone: a low mound in a deserted corner of the old city.

landmarks.summary: The westernmost Buddhist sanctuary excavated in Central Asia: a mud-brick stupa and a monastery round a court in the south-east corner of Gyaur Kala, in use about the 4th–6th centuries.
details: Soviet excavators found the stupa, a monastery of cells round a court and a sanctuary with a large clay Buddha head. In the stupa lay a vase holding Buddhist texts in Sanskrit on birch bark. It shows Buddhists living in Sasanian Merv beside Zoroastrians and Christians.
The miniature shows a square stepped base, a dome (anda) with a harmika and parasols, and the monastery's ring of cells. Its height and the finish of the dome are reconstructed.

landmarks.name: Erk Kala

achaemenid-500.name: Erk Kala, citadel of Margu
achaemenid-500.note: The round fortress of the satrapy of Margiana: a high mud-brick wall on its rampart, the governor's hall, granaries and houses.

sasanian-500.name: Erk Kala, citadel of Marw
sasanian-500.note: Now the citadel on the north side of Gyaur Kala, seat of the marzban, the Sasanian governor of the frontier.

seljuk-1100.name: Erk Kala (abandoned)
seljuk-1100.note: The government has moved to the Shahriyar Ark; the old citadel is a high, empty ring of ramparts.

ruins-1250.name: Erk Kala (ruins)
ruins-1250.note: A ring of eroded earth over the deserted old city.

timurid-1450.name: Erk Kala (ruins)
timurid-1450.note: A grass-grown ring of ramparts, used as a lookout by herders.

landmarks.summary: The oldest of Merv's cities: a round citadel of about 20 hectares on a high rampart, founded in the Achaemenid period and later the citadel of Gyaur Kala.
details: Erk Kala was probably built in the 6th century BCE as the fortress of Margu, the Achaemenid province named at Behistun. Its walls were raised again and again on their own ruins until the ramparts rose about 30 metres above the plain. The Sasanian governors still ruled from it.

The miniature shows the ring wall on its rampart with towers, a gate, the governor's hall, granaries and houses inside. The buildings inside are a reconstruction; the ruined variant is the ring of ramparts that survives.
landmarks.built: 6th century BCE, rebuilt to the 7th century CE

landmarks.name: Great Kyz Kala

sasanian-500.note: Probably not yet built: dates proposed for the Kyz Kalas run from the 6th to the 9th century.

seljuk-1100.note: An old koshk outside the west wall of the Seljuk city, perhaps still lived in by a landowning family.

ruins-1250.note: Abandoned; its upper floor and roof timbers gone, the corrugated walls still standing.

timurid-1450.note: Already an old ruin with a legend: the 'Maidens' Castle'.

landmarks.summary: The 'Great Maidens' Castle': a fortified two-storey manor (koshk) of mud brick about 42 by 37 metres, its walls ribbed with tall half-round corrugations.
details: The Great Kyz Kala stands on a high sloping plinth. Its outer walls are formed by closely packed half-columns of mud brick, which strengthened the walls and gave them their striking corrugated look. Inside, two storeys of rooms surround a small court. Its date is debated: proposals run from the 6th to the 9th century.
The miniature shows the plinth, the corrugated walls, a ramp to the door and the court. The upper parapet is reconstructed.

landmarks.name: Small Kyz Kala

sasanian-500.note: Probably not yet built; the estates of dihqans dot the oasis.

seljuk-1100.note: The smaller koshk beside the Great Kyz Kala, close to the Hurmuzfarra canal.

timurid-1450.note: A crumbling ruin beside its larger neighbour.

landmarks.summary: The smaller of the two 'Maidens' Castles', a corrugated-walled koshk near the Great Kyz Kala.
details: Built in the same way as its larger neighbour, with corrugated mud-brick walls on a plinth and rooms round a central space, but much smaller. Koshks like these were the fortified homes of landowners throughout the oasis.
The miniature uses the same corrugated-wall technique on a smaller body; its height is approximate.

landmarks.name: Mausoleum of Muhammad ibn Zayd

sasanian-500.note: Fields north of the later walls.

seljuk-1100.note: Newly built in 1112–1113 over the grave of an Alid saint, north of the city walls; a place of pilgrimage.

ruins-1250.note: Spared, or soon repaired: a shrine with a keeper amid the abandoned northern suburbs.

timurid-1450.note: Still a shrine, later remodelled with a new entrance.

landmarks.summary: A small Seljuk mausoleum of fired brick dated by its inscription to 1112–1113, over the grave of a descendant of the Prophet called Muhammad ibn Zayd.
details: A square domed chamber with a deep entrance, built of fine fired brick; a band of Kufic inscription in carved brick gives the date. Which Muhammad ibn Zayd lies here is unclear; the shrine has been venerated ever since.
The miniature shows the square chamber, the dome on its octagonal zone and the inscription band. Later additions are left out.

landmarks.name: Ice house (yakhdan)

seljuk-1100.note: One of several ice houses round the city, storing winter ice for the summer drinks of the rich.

ruins-1250.note: Derelict: the shade wall slumping, the ice pit full of sand.

timurid-1450.note: In use again as the canals run once more.

landmarks.summary: A conical domed ice house of mud brick: water from the canal froze in shallow pools on winter nights, shaded by a high wall, and the ice was stacked in a deep pit under the dome.
details: Several ice houses survive round Merv, with steep stepped domes of mud brick over pits several metres deep. Their dates are hard to fix and some may be quite late; ice houses of this kind were used across Iran and Central Asia for centuries.
The miniature shows the conical dome, its door, the freezing pools and the long shade wall to the south of them. The pairing with this era is an interpretation.

landmarks.name: Askhab Mausolea

ruins-1250.note: Two graves of Companions of the Prophet, visited by pilgrims among the ruins; no great buildings yet.

timurid-1450.note: Two tall Timurid iwans now stand behind the graves of al-Hakam and Buraydah, and a small mosque serves the pilgrims.

landmarks.summary: The graves of two Companions of the Prophet who died at Merv, al-Hakam ibn Amr al-Ghifari and Buraydah ibn al-Husayb, framed by two Timurid iwans.
details: The two Companions came with the Arab armies and died at Merv in the 7th century. In the 15th century two great brick portals (iwans) were built behind their tombs, which stand in the open before them.
The miniature shows the twin iwans with tiled frames and the two raised tombs on a paved terrace. The tile colours are simplified.

landmarks.name: Walls of Abdullah Khan Kala (north gate)

ruins-1250.note: Open, half-abandoned fields south of the ruined Seljuk city.

timurid-1450.note: The new walls of Shah Rukh's town, fresh mud brick on a pakhsa base, with a gate facing the old cities to the north.

landmarks.summary: The walls of the Timurid town founded south of the old cities, by the usual account in 1409, later named after the 16th-century Uzbek khan Abdullah.
details: Shah Rukh, ruling from Herat, had the Murghab dam rebuilt and a new town laid out. Its walls enclose a rough square of some 600 metres with towers and gates; a citadel stood in one corner. In the 18th century Bairam Ali Khan Kala was added beside it.
The miniature shows a stretch of wall with round towers and a gate with a pointed arch. The date of 1409 and the gate design are hedged.

landmarks.name: Weir of the Majan canal

sasanian-500.note: An earlier timber and brushwood weir regulated the canal here.

seljuk-1100.note: A brick weir with sluices where the mir-ab's men measured the city's share of water.

ruins-1250.note: Broken: the canals silt up and the oasis shrinks.

timurid-1450.note: Rebuilt as part of Shah Rukh's restoration of the irrigation.

landmarks.summary: A brick weir and sluices on the Majan canal south of the city, standing for the water works that made Merv possible.
details: All of Merv lived on the Murghab's water, divided by dams and weirs into the four canals. Istakhri says the official in charge of water had some 10,000 workers, more than the governor. Where exactly the Majan's sluices stood is not known.

The miniature shows a brick weir across the canal with sluice gates, a gatekeeper's hut and stores of brushwood. It is an interpretation built from descriptions of water control, not a known structure.

spots.name: A Margian farmstead
spots.summary: A walled farmstead on a canal south of Erk Kala, where a family grows barley and vines and owes a share of the harvest to the king's storehouse.
details: Margiana had been farmed by canal irrigation for well over a thousand years before the Persians came. Under the Achaemenids its farmers paid tax in kind to the citadel; the Behistun inscription shows the province could raise a whole army in revolt.

vignettes.text: The father lifts the sluice board on the family's channel; water slides over the barley as the sun clears the desert edge.
Under a reed shade the women grind grain on a saddle quern; a tax clerk from the citadel tallies jars of grain on a clay tablet.
Doors barred against wolves and raiders; the dog barks at a caravan's bells far off on the road to Aria.

spots.name: Church of the metropolitan of Marw
spots.summary: A mud-brick church north-west of the city walls, seat of the bishop (later metropolitan) of Marw of the Church of the East.
details: Bishops of Merv are recorded at the synods of the Church of the East from 424; Merv became a metropolitan see and sent missionaries to the Turks. A building outside the walls at Kharoba Koshuk is often identified as a church; this spot follows that suggestion.

vignettes.text: The night office ends; deacons chant in Syriac by lamplight, and the bishop blesses a merchant leaving for Sogdiana.
In the yard a scribe copies the Psalms; a Persian convert waits nervously to be baptised, knowing apostasy from Zoroastrianism can be punished.
A wooden clapper (the semantron) calls the monks to the evening prayer; candles flicker before a painted cross.

spots.name: Fire temple
spots.summary: A domed fire temple in the north-east quarter of Gyaur Kala, where priests keep the sacred fire burning day and night.
details: Zoroastrianism was the religion of the Sasanian state; Merv had fire temples and Zoroastrian ossuary burials have been found round the city. The exact place of a temple inside Gyaur Kala is not known, so this spot is placed for illustration.

vignettes.text: A priest with a cloth over his mouth, so his breath does not pollute the flame, feeds sandalwood and dry tamarisk to the fire.
A family brings a gift of wood and incense after a birth; the priest recites the Avesta in a language no one else understands.
Only the fire's glow through the doorway; the sound of chanting in the dark courtyard.

spots.name: Monk with the birch-bark sutras
spots.summary: A Buddhist monk in the monastery by the stupa, copying and reciting Sanskrit texts written on birch bark.
details: A vase buried in the stupa of Gyaur Kala held Buddhist texts in Sanskrit on birch bark, and a large clay Buddha head was found in the sanctuary. Monks here were part of a network reaching Bactria and Gandhara.

vignettes.text: Barefoot monks walk round the stupa clockwise, murmuring; the dome glows pale in the first light.
In a cell a monk smooths a strip of birch bark and copies a sutra in Brahmi script, brought from Bactria.
Butter lamps in the niches of the stupa; a merchant from Termez leaves coins for the community and asks for a safe road.

spots.name: The library of the Friday mosque
spots.summary: One of the ten endowed libraries Yaqut counted in Merv shortly before 1221, kept by the Friday mosque.
details: Yaqut spent about three years in Merv before the Mongols came and wrote that he had never seen libraries like them: ten waqf libraries, one at the Friday mosque (called the Aziziyya) with some 12,000 volumes. He could borrow up to 200 books at a time without a pledge, he says.

vignettes.text: The librarian unlocks the cupboards; the smell of paper and glue. Volumes lie flat in piles, labelled on their edges.
A geographer from Hama carries home an armful of books on donkeyback, signing nothing: the endowment trusts its readers.
Lamps out by order, for fear of fire; a student copies the last line of a hadith collection by moonlight in the court.

ruins-1250.note: Burned or scattered in 1221; Yaqut, who left just in time, mourned the books.

spots.name: Silk-weavers' workshop
spots.summary: A courtyard workshop where silk raised in the oasis is reeled, dyed and woven on drawlooms.
details: The geographers say Merv raised silkworms and exported silk and cocoons; mulberry trees lined its canals. Merv's weavers also made fine cotton cloth. Workshops of this kind are reconstructed from the texts and from finds of spindles and dye vats.

vignettes.text: Cocoons simmer in a copper pot; a girl draws the thread out onto a reel while the steam fogs the cold morning air.
On the drawloom a boy perched above lifts the pattern cords while the master weaver throws the shuttle: paired birds in roundels.
Skeins dyed madder-red hang drying in the court; the master counts bolts promised to a merchant from Baghdad.

spots.name: Caravanserai of the Nishapur gate
spots.summary: A fortified inn outside the west gate where caravans on the Khurasan road unload: rooms round a court, stables behind.
details: Merv sat on the Great Khurasan Road from Baghdad to Transoxiana and China and on the route south to Herat and India. The Seljuks built caravanserais along the roads; this one is placed for illustration outside the western gate.

vignettes.text: Camels groan to their feet in the court; drivers load bales of Merv cotton and sacks of dried melon for Baghdad.
A money-changer weighs dinars from Nishapur against Seljuk silver; a Jewish merchant from Isfahan writes a letter of credit.
Gate barred, a fire in the court; a traveller from Kashgar tells of the Kara Khitai, whose armies will soon matter very much.

spots.name: Office of the mir-ab
spots.summary: The office of the amir of water on the Majan, who decided how much of the Murghab each canal and village could take.
details: Istakhri and Ibn Hawqal report that Merv's water was shared by careful measure, with the mir-ab commanding some 10,000 men to guard the dams and clean the canals, more than the governor had. How the shares were measured in detail is not recorded.

vignettes.text: The mir-ab reads the river gauge brought by a rider from the dam: the Murghab is low; every share will be cut by a quarter.
Village headmen argue before his bench; one is accused of breaking a sluice by night to water his melons.
Crews with spades and baskets set out to clear silt from the Razik by torchlight before the next water turn.

spots.name: Melon fields of the Majan
spots.summary: Melon beds in the irrigated fields south of the city; Merv's melons were dried in strips and sent as far as Baghdad.
details: Medieval geographers praised Merv's melons: sliced and dried, they were exported to Iraq. Melons need sweet water and hot summers, and the Murghab oasis has both. The detail of dried melon for the caliph's table is told of Khwarazm and Merv alike.

vignettes.text: The grower walks the furrows thumping melons and listening; ripe ones go to the city by donkey before the heat.
Under a reed shelter his daughters cut melons into long strips and hang them to dry on poles like yellow ribbons.
A boy sleeps in a lookout on stilts, a sling at his side, guarding the beds from jackals and thieves.

timurid-1450.note: Melon beds again, on land brought back to water by Shah Rukh's restored canals.

spots.name: The sultan's observatory
spots.summary: Where astronomers of the Seljuk court observed the sky; al-Khazini compiled his Sanjari tables at Merv, and Omar Khayyam is said to have worked here too.
details: Under Malik Shah, Khayyam led the astronomers who reformed the calendar (the Jalali calendar, 1079), probably at Isfahan. Merv had an observatory under Sanjar, where al-Khazini wrote the Zij al-Sanjari and his Book of the Balance of Wisdom. That Khayyam worked in Merv is reported but not certain; the site is unknown.

vignettes.text: Al-Khazini notes the sun's rising point against a marked wall, then weighs a lump of gold in water on his great balance.
Clerks recompute planetary tables for the Sanjari zij; an astrologer asks for a lucky hour for the sultan's hunt.
On the roof an old astronomer sights a star through a brass alidade; somebody quotes a quatrain on the turning wheel of heaven.

spots.name: Bazaar of the cloth sellers
spots.summary: A domed market street by the Majan where Merv's famous fine cotton cloth ('marwi') was sold by the bale.
details: Merv was known across the caliphate for its cotton, woven so fine that 'marwi' cloth was a byword, much like muslin later. Silk, felt, copper and the dried fruit of the oasis also passed through its markets.

vignettes.text: Shutters come down; a broker shakes out a length of white cotton so thin the sunlight shows through.
Under the dome the muhtasib checks a cloth-seller's yardstick against the market standard; a bale goes to a Baghdad agent.
Lanes empty; watchmen walk with lanterns; a cat sleeps on a pile of folded turbans.

spots.name: Herders in the ruins
spots.summary: A few families of herders and farmers living in patched-up rooms among the empty courtyards of Sultan Kala.
details: After the massacre of 1221 Merv never recovered its size. Excavations show small-scale occupation in parts of Sultan Kala in the Ilkhanid period, people reusing old houses and brick among the ruins.

vignettes.text: Sheep spill out of a roofless courtyard that was once a merchant's house; the shepherd's wife milks a goat by the old pool.
A boy digs in a mound and finds a green-glazed bowl, unbroken; his mother uses it for curds.
Wind moans in the empty gate; far off, the dome of Sanjar's tomb stands black against the stars.

spots.name: Keeper of the ice house
spots.summary: The keeper who floods the freezing pools on winter nights, cuts the ice and sells it in summer to the town's sherbet-makers.
details: In an ice house (yakhdan) shallow pools were flooded on cold nights and shaded from the sun by a tall wall; the ice was cut and stored under a mud-brick dome, insulated with straw, until summer. The method is well documented in Iran and Central Asia.

vignettes.text: January: the keeper breaks the night's ice in the pools with a mallet and slides the slabs down into the pit under the dome.
July: he climbs down into the cold, cuts a block wrapped in straw and sells it to a sherbet-seller from the bazaar.
Winter again: he opens the canal sluice and lets water spread thin over the pools before the frost.

spots.name: Bazaar of the new town
spots.summary: The crossing of the two streets of Shah Rukh's town, where farmers, Turkmen herders and Herat merchants meet.
details: The Timurid town was a modest place compared with Sanjar's capital: a market town of the Herat kingdom on the road north, living on the restored oasis. Its bazaar is reconstructed after other Timurid towns.

vignettes.text: A miller's cart of flour, a baker's tandoor already hot, Turkmen boys driving sheep in through the Herat gate.
A Herat merchant sells paper and blue-and-white bowls; a mason buys old Seljuk bricks carted from the ruins.
The town gate shuts; a storyteller in the teahouse-like porch recites from the Shahnameh to men on felt rugs.

events.title: Margiana rises under Frada
events.text: As Darius fought for the throne, Margiana rebelled and made a man called Frada its king. The satrap of Bactria, Dadarshi, marched on Margu and crushed the revolt. The Behistun inscription boasts of tens of thousands dead (the Babylonian version gives over 55,000); royal numbers, but a sign of a populous oasis.

events.title: Antiochus founds Antiochia Margiana
events.text: Pliny says Alexander founded a city here which was destroyed, and Antiochus I rebuilt it as Antiochia; Strabo adds that Antiochus walled the whole oasis. The square city of Gyaur Kala, laid out round Erk Kala, is its trace on the ground.

events.title: Merv opens its gates to the Arabs
events.text: The marzban Mahoye surrenders Merv by treaty to the army of Abdallah ibn Amir, paying tribute. Merv becomes the Arab base for Khurasan; in 671 some 50,000 Arab families from Basra and Kufa are settled in the oasis.

events.title: The last Sasanian king killed
events.text: Yazdegerd III, fleeing the Arabs, reached Merv, where the marzban turned against him. The usual story says he hid in a mill on a canal near the city and was killed by the miller for his rich clothes. Christians of Merv are said to have buried him.

events.title: Abu Muslim raises the black banners
events.text: In a village of the Merv oasis Abu Muslim unfurls black banners for the family of the Prophet, launching the Abbasid revolution. Merv falls to him early in 748. He builds a palace and mosque on the Majan canal, the start of the new city to the west.

events.title: Al-Ma'mun rules the caliphate from Merv
events.text: Harun al-Rashid's son al-Ma'mun governs Khurasan from Merv, defeats his brother al-Amin in the civil war and for some years rules the whole caliphate from here before moving to Baghdad in 819.

events.title: The Seljuks take Merv
events.text: Turkmen horsemen under Chaghri Beg occupy Merv; in 1040 the Seljuks defeat the Ghaznavid army at Dandanaqan, between Merv and Sarakhs, and make Khurasan theirs. Merv becomes the seat of the Seljuk rulers of the east.

events.title: Sanjar becomes Great Sultan
events.text: Ahmad Sanjar, ruler of Khurasan from Merv since 1097, becomes supreme sultan of the Seljuks. For four decades Merv is the capital of an empire from Iraq to Transoxiana, crowded with poets, scholars and astronomers.

events.title: The Oghuz capture Sanjar
events.text: Oghuz tribesmen, angered by tax collectors, defeat and capture the old sultan and sack Merv. Sanjar is held captive for about three years, taken round with the tribes; he escapes in 1156, returns to a ruined capital and dies the next year.

events.title: Sanjar laid in his mausoleum
events.text: Sanjar dies in May 1157 and is buried in the great domed tomb at the heart of Sultan Kala. With him the Seljuk empire of the east breaks apart; Merv passes to the Khwarazm-shahs.

events.title: Tolui destroys Merv
events.text: Tolui's army surrounds Merv; the governor surrenders on a promise of mercy. The people are led onto the plain over four days, craftsmen set aside, the rest killed. Chroniclers give 700,000 or 1.3 million dead, impossible figures that show the horror. The city burns.

events.title: Shah Rukh refounds Merv
events.text: Timur's son Shah Rukh, ruling from Herat, orders the Murghab dam rebuilt and a new town laid out south of the old ruins. Water returns to the oasis; the town later takes the name of Abdullah Khan, the 16th-century Uzbek ruler.

stories.title: A day in Sanjar's capital
stories.summary: Walk through Seljuk Merv at its height: from the sultan's citadel to the bazaars, the libraries and the mausoleum where Sanjar will lie.

steps.title: The sultan's court
steps.text: In the Ark the court gathers round Sanjar. His panegyrist Anvari, perhaps the finest court poet of the age, recites a qasida comparing the sultan to the sun; the vizier counts the cost.

steps.title: Watching the sky
steps.text: Astronomers measure the heavens for the Sanjari tables, and al-Khazini weighs metals on his balance to tell gold from fakes.

steps.title: The cloth market
steps.text: Down by the Majan, merchants handle cotton so fine it is sold across the caliphate under the name of Merv.

steps.title: The weavers
steps.text: In a courtyard nearby, steaming cocoons, the clack of the drawloom, and bolts of patterned silk for Baghdad and the court.

steps.title: The libraries
steps.text: In the Friday mosque the library lends books by the armful; seventy years later Yaqut will borrow 200 at a time.

steps.title: The great tomb
steps.text: Beside the mosque the brick cube and its towering double dome go up; the sultan is laid here after his captivity among the Oghuz.

stories.title: Marw of many faiths
stories.summary: Within one wall in Sasanian Merv: a fire temple, a Christian church, a Buddhist stupa and the governor's citadel.

steps.title: Through the south gate
steps.text: Caravans from Herat enter under the towers of the square city that Antiochus founded eight centuries before.

steps.title: The sacred fire
steps.text: In the north-east quarter priests feed the fire of the state religion, the faith of the King of Kings.

steps.title: The stupa
steps.text: In the south-east corner Buddhist monks walk round their mud-brick stupa, the farthest west of their monasteries in Central Asia.

steps.title: Sutras on birch bark
steps.text: A monk copies a Sanskrit text on birch bark, the kind later found buried in a vase inside the stupa.

steps.title: The bishop's church
steps.text: Outside the walls Christians of the Church of the East sing in Syriac; their bishops will soon carry the faith to the Turks.

steps.title: The marzban's citadel
steps.text: On the high round rampart of Erk Kala the Persian governor keeps the frontier, as his predecessors did for a thousand years.
